title: Brain Injury in Football: Concussions, Repeated Impacts, and CTE
takeaways: Diagnosis requires the characteristic neuronal phosphorylated-tau lesion around small vessels at cortical sulcal depths; symptoms and photographs cannot establish it in a living player.
Football includes diagnosed concussions and repeated impacts without recognized symptoms. Exposure estimates and selected brain donations do not directly establish population prevalence.
Axons and tau have normal functions.
Spectrin, actin, microtubules, and tau support axonal mechanics, transport, and synaptic organization. Pathological modification and assembly can disturb these functions.
CTE involves more than tau deposits.

Human studies identify selective neuronal loss, white-matter changes, vascular responses, and altered immune-cell states. These measurements test different aspects of neuronal survival and tissue function.
Cell cultures, worms, fish, mice, and human tissue preparations isolate mechanisms. A model of seeding, clearance, or injury is not automatically a model that reproduces CTE.
Clinical evidence must match the claim.

Current biomarkers can reflect other pathology, including Alzheimer disease. Exposure reduction, concussion care, and treatment of symptoms remain important while CTE-specific diagnostics and therapies are investigated.
